title: Full-Rank Noise Forbids Long-Range Entanglement Swapping
authors: Xuan Du Trinh, Nicholas Pardave, Angie Huang, Xiangyi Meng, Nengkun Yu
abstract: Quantum repeaters extend entanglement by swapping noisy elementary links. We prove that full-rank noise forbids this at long range: for any entangled full-rank two-qubit link, there is a finite depth beyond which no end-to-end entanglement can be established regardless of the measurement outcomes on intermediate qubits, even under any adaptive postselected strategy. This limit is set by one spectral parameter of the link, giving a no-go criterion for repeater routing. In contrast, we construct link state families of rank three and rank two that admit postselected measurement outcome branches of exponentially small probability but with strictly positive concurrence at every finite depth. Swapping experiments on a superconducting processor show that links of equal initial concurrence but different rank behave differently under postselected swapping. In the language of many-body physics, the chain is a matrix-product density operator, and full-rank bonds forbid long-range localizable entanglement, while rank-deficient bonds can sustain it.
summary: This work establishes a fundamental difference in entanglement persistence based on the rank of noise in quantum repeater links. Full-rank noise inevitably leads to a finite 'entanglement horizon,' while rank-deficient links can sustain entanglement indefinitely through specific postselection strategies. This has implications for designing robust quantum networks.
main_problem: The paper investigates whether long-range entanglement can be established using quantum repeaters when the elementary links are corrupted by full-rank noise, especially under adaptive postselection.
main_result: Full-rank noise imposes a finite 'entanglement horizon' beyond which entanglement swapping fails, whereas rank-deficient links can sustain entanglement indefinitely on specific postselected branches.
method: The authors use the Choi operator formalism and analyze the decay of the end-to-end state by comparing the behavior of full-rank versus low-rank link channels.
model_or_system: The system models quantum repeaters extending entanglement over noisy two-qubit links, analyzed using concepts from matrix-product density operators in many-body physics.
key_observables: Concurrence, the entanglement horizon, and the network 'score' $\beta(P)$ are key observables used to quantify entanglement decay.
important_parameters: The link rank (full vs. low), the noise parameter $\eta$, and the depth $N$ of the repeater chain are crucial parameters.
main_assumptions: The analysis often relies on reducing the full-rank problem to an isotropic chain model, and some derivations use approximations for small noise/storage loads.
figures_summary: Figure 2 compares the decay of concurrence for full-rank (DP) versus rank-deficient (AD) channels, showing the theoretical distinction between the two noise types.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the finite horizon for full-rank links (Theorem 1) to constructing low-rank counterexamples, and finally analyzing the role of storage and purification in maintaining entanglement.
why_interesting: The distinction between full-rank and low-rank noise provides a powerful, physically motivated criterion for the feasibility of long-distance quantum communication, linking quantum information theory to the structure of quantum channels.

The N + 1 links ρ0 oc- cupy the qubit pairs (Ai, Bi), and intermediate node i post- selects the entangled outcome |Ψi⟩= (I ⊗Mi) |Φ+⟩on its pair (Bi−1, Ai). Tracing out the measured qubits leaves the state ρN of the boundary pair A0BN, in which each outcome enters as the filter map Mi(X) = M ∗ i XM T i . The outcomes |Ψi⟩need not be Bell states or maximally entangled. Postse- lection keeps only the branch with the intended record {Mi}, and the rule choosing each measurement may adapt to the outcomes already observed.

FIG. 2. Experimental verification of rank-aware distinction in entanglement swapping. The states are prepared under one- sided, rank-2 amplitude-damping (AD) and rank-4 depolariz- ing (DP) channels respectively on IBM’s Heron R3 processor (ibm boston), with an initial concurrence C(AD) ≈C(DP) ≈ 0.7. The ratio monotonically decays to zero (solid), signaling the sudden death of C(DP) as the theory predicts (dashed). Eventually both C(DP) and C(AD) reach zero due to exper- imental imperfection (inset).
